subtype: Approach: everyone trying random fixes at once [Pitfall]
passage:
Tuesday: The reporting service slowed to a crawl and five engineers jumped in. Alka raised the cache limit. Lakshmi restarted two servers. Others changed a timeout, cleared a queue and edited a config file, none of them saying so in the chat.

Wednesday: The service was worse, then better, then worse again. Alka asked, 'Who touched the timeout?' Three people thought someone else had. Nobody could say which change had helped or which had made things wobble, and two changes were undone by guesswork.

Friday: In the review, Lakshmi said, 'We fixed it and can't explain how.' The cost was two extra days of customer complaints and a late report to the client. They agreed that any change would be announced in the chat before anyone made it.

qa.q: How many engineers jumped in on Tuesday?
What was Alka feeling when asking who had touched the timeout?
qa.a: Alka was confused and probably anxious, since nobody could tell which change had done what.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team have used?
qa.a: One person could have made one change at a time and announced it, so the effect of each change could be seen.

qa.q: How might the client have seen the outage?
qa.a: The client saw slow service and a late report, and was probably frustrated by a problem that lasted longer than it needed to.

grounding: Shows several engineers changing settings at once without telling each other, so nobody can tell which change helped or hurt.

subtype: Approach: everyone trying random fixes at once [Pitfall]
passage: Leela, you asked why I get so strict when an outage starts. Your Saurabh sir learnt the hard way. I was twenty-five, in a team of five, when our order system slowed to a crawl one evening. We all panicked at once. I increased the memory. My friend restarted the cache. Someone else changed a timeout. Another rolled back a config. Nobody told anyone. After an hour, the system got better for ten minutes, then worse. Which change helped? Which hurt? We had no idea. We couldn't even say what state the servers were in anymore. It took until four in the morning, and we had to undo everything and start over, one change at a time. So when I say 'one person changes things, and says it out loud', that's why.

qa.q: Until what time did the outage go on?
How did Saurabh feel when the system improved for ten minutes and then got worse?
qa.a: He felt confused and helpless, unable to tell which change had helped or hurt.

qa.q: What choice early that evening could have saved the night?
qa.a: If one person had made changes one at a time and announced each, the team would have known which change helped.

qa.q: How might Saurabh's friend who restarted the cache have felt by four in the morning?
qa.a: The friend was likely exhausted and frustrated, having tried to help but adding to the confusion.

grounding: It shows a team where several engineers change settings at once without telling one another, so no one can tell which change helped or hurt.

subtype: Approach: everyone trying random fixes at once [Pitfall]
passage:
The festival sale started at midnight, and at 12.04 the checkout began to time out. Five engineers jumped into the call from five homes. Alka, on call for only her second time, watched the channel fill: 'restarting pods', 'bumping the pool size', 'turning off the cache', 'scaling to twenty', 'rolling back the promo service'. Nobody waited for anyone.
At 12.20 errors dropped. At 12.25 they doubled. 'What did someone just change?' Naveen shouted. Three people answered at once. Nobody knew the current state of the system anymore; half the changes contradicted each other.
At 1.30 a senior finally took charge, froze all changes and started again, one at a time. The fix turned out to be one setting. The sale had lost ninety minutes of its busiest night.

qa.q: At what time did the checkout begin to time out?
What might Alka have been feeling as the channel filled?
qa.a: She was probably overwhelmed and anxious, new to on-call and watching changes pile up with nobody coordinating.

qa.q: What would you change first in how this team responds?
qa.a: Name one person in charge at the start and allow one change at a time, announced in the channel before it happens.

qa.q: How did customers experience the night?
qa.a: Shoppers couldn't check out for much of ninety minutes on the busiest sale night, which likely cost sales and goodwill.

grounding: It shows five engineers changing settings at once without telling one another, so the system state becomes unclear and no one knows which change helped.
